front: A routine executes the nested loop: for \(i = 1\) to \(n\), and for each \(i\), for \(j = 1\) to \(n\), perform one constant-time operation. What is the routine's time complexity in Big-O notation?
explanation: 1) The outer loop runs \(n\) times. 2) For every outer iteration the inner loop runs \(n\) times. 3) Total operations \(= n \times n = n^2\). 4) Keeping the dominant term gives \(O(n^2)\).

front: Starting from \(i = 1\), a loop repeatedly executes \(i = i \times 2\) as long as \(i < n\). How many iterations does it run, expressed in Big-O of \(n\)?
explanation: 1) After successive iterations \(i\) takes the values \(1, 2, 4, \dots, 2^k\). 2) The loop stops once \(2^k \ge n\). 3) Solving \(2^k \ge n\) gives \(k \ge \log_2 n\). 4) So it runs about \(\log_2 n\) times, i.e. \(O(\log n)\).

front: An algorithm's running time is \(T(n) = 3n^2 + 5n\log n + 100n + 2000\). Give its asymptotic time complexity in Big-O notation.
explanation: 1) Big-O keeps only the fastest-growing term and drops constant factors. 2) For large \(n\), \(n^2 > n\log n > n > 1\). 3) The dominant term is \(3n^2\). 4) Dropping the constant \(3\) gives \(O(n^2)\).

front: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort when sorting a list of \(n\) elements?
explanation: 1) Merge sort recursively splits the list in half, producing \(\log_2 n\) levels of division. 2) At each level, merging all sublists touches every element once, i.e. \(O(n)\) work. 3) Total work \(= n \times \log_2 n\). 4) Hence \(O(n\log n)\).

front: What is the worst-case time complexity of bubble sort when sorting a list of \(n\) elements?
explanation: 1) Bubble sort makes repeated passes, comparing adjacent elements. 2) In the worst case it needs about \(n\) passes. 3) Each pass performs up to \(n-1\) comparisons. 4) Total comparisons \(\approx n(n-1)\), giving \(O(n^2)\).

front: What is the time complexity of reading the element stored at a known index of an array?
explanation: 1) An array occupies contiguous memory. 2) The address of element \(i\) is computed directly as \(\text{base} + i \times (\text{element size})\). 3) This is a single constant-time calculation regardless of array size. 4) Therefore access is \(O(1)\).

front: The items \(A, B, C, D\) are pushed onto an initially empty stack in that order. After two pop operations, which item is on top of the stack?
explanation: 1) A stack is LIFO (last in, first out). 2) After pushing, the order from top to bottom is \(D, C, B, A\). 3) The first pop removes \(D\); the second pop removes \(C\). 4) The item now on top is \(B\).

front: The values \(3, 8, 5, 1\) are enqueued into an initially empty queue in that order. After two dequeue operations, which value is at the front of the queue?
explanation: 1) A queue is FIFO (first in, first out). 2) The order from front to back is \(3, 8, 5, 1\). 3) The first dequeue removes \(3\); the second removes \(8\). 4) The value now at the front is \(5\).

1) Read left to right, pushing operands: the stack holds \(5\), then \(3\). 2) The \(+\) pops \(3\) and \(5\) and pushes \(5 + 3 = 8\). 3) Push \(2\); the \(\times\) pops \(2\) and \(8\) and pushes \(8 \times 2 = 16\). 4) The result is \(16\).

front: How many total nodes are in a perfect binary tree of \(4\) levels (root at level 1, every level completely filled)?
explanation: 1) Level \(k\) of a perfect binary tree holds \(2^{k-1}\) nodes. 2) Levels 1 through 4 hold \(1, 2, 4, 8\) nodes. 3) Sum \(= 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15\). 4) Equivalently \(2^4 - 1 = 15\).

front: What is the time complexity of inserting a new node at the head (front) of a singly linked list, given a pointer to the head?
explanation: 1) Create the new node. 2) Set its next field to the current head. 3) Update the head pointer to the new node. 4) These are a fixed number of operations independent of list length, so \(O(1)\).

front: Trace the pseudocode \(n = 20,\ \text{count} = 0\); while \(n > 1\): \(n = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\), \(\text{count} = \text{count} + 1\). What is the final value of \(\text{count}\)?
explanation: 1) \(n = 20 \to 10\), count \(= 1\). 2) \(n = 10 \to 5\), count \(= 2\). 3) \(n = 5 \to 2\), count \(= 3\). 4) \(n = 2 \to 1\), count \(= 4\); now \(n = 1\) fails \(n > 1\), so the loop ends with count \(= 4\).

front: Trace the pseudocode \(\text{sum} = 0\); for \(k = 1\) to \(5\): \(\text{sum} = \text{sum} + k\). What is the final value of \(\text{sum}\)?
explanation: 1) The loop adds each integer \(k\) from 1 to 5 to sum. 2) Running total: \(1, 3, 6, 10, 15\). 3) This equals \(\tfrac{5 \times 6}{2} = 15\). 4) The final sum is \(15\).

front: Trace the pseudocode \(\text{total} = 0\); for \(i = 1\) to \(6\): if \(i\) is even, \(\text{total} = \text{total} + i\). What is the final value of \(\text{total}\)?
explanation: 1) Only even values of \(i\) contribute. 2) The even values in \(1 \dots 6\) are \(2, 4, 6\). 3) Sum \(= 2 + 4 + 6 = 12\). 4) The final total is \(12\).

front: Given \(A = \text{true}\), \(B = \text{false}\), \(C = \text{true}\), evaluate \((A \text{ AND } B)\ \text{OR}\ (\text{NOT } B \text{ AND } C)\).
explanation: 1) \(A \text{ AND } B = \text{true AND false} = \text{false}\). 2) \(\text{NOT } B = \text{true}\), so \(\text{NOT } B \text{ AND } C = \text{true AND true} = \text{true}\). 3) \(\text{false OR true} = \text{true}\). 4) The expression evaluates to true.

front: Use De Morgan's law to rewrite \(\text{NOT}(A \text{ OR } B)\) so that the negation is not applied to the whole expression.
explanation: 1) De Morgan's law states \(\overline{A + B} = \bar{A} \cdot \bar{B}\). 2) The negation of an OR becomes an AND of the negations. 3) Thus \(\text{NOT}(A \text{ OR } B) = (\text{NOT } A) \text{ AND } (\text{NOT } B)\).

front: A function is defined recursively as \(f(n) = 1\) if \(n \le 1\), otherwise \(f(n) = n \times f(n-1)\). What is \(f(4)\)?
explanation: 1) \(f(4) = 4 \times f(3)\). 2) Expanding: \(f(3) = 3 \times f(2)\), \(f(2) = 2 \times f(1)\), \(f(1) = 1\). 3) Multiplying back up: \(4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24\). 4) This is \(4! = 24\).

front: A function is defined recursively as \(\text{fib}(n) = n\) if \(n < 2\), otherwise \(\text{fib}(n) = \text{fib}(n-1) + \text{fib}(n-2)\). What is \(\text{fib}(6)\)?

What is the worst-case time complexity of computing the \(n\)-th Fibonacci number using the naive doubly-recursive definition \(\text{fib}(n) = \text{fib}(n-1) + \text{fib}(n-2)\), with no memoization?
explanation: 1) Each call to \(\text{fib}(n)\) spawns two further calls. 2) This forms a recursion tree whose number of nodes roughly doubles at each level down to depth \(n\). 3) The number of calls grows exponentially, bounded above by \(O(2^n)\). 4) This is why memoization or an iterative approach is preferred.
